lead: Quality function deployment (QFD) is a planning method that starts with customer needs and ends with ranked technical responses. Customers say what they want: tasty food, quick service, low price. Engineers list how they can act: change the menu cycle, add serving counters. A relationship matrix rates how strongly each how supports each what. Importance weights turn those ratings into priority scores. The team builds what ranks high first. QFD is used in product design, services and software. Only a few universities teach it.
prereq: You need 2.1 Functional and non-functional requirements and 2.5 SRS scope; basic multiplication is enough.

blocks.text: QFD begins with customer needs, called the whats. Collect them from users, not from one manager. In a hostel mess, students ask for tasty food, quick service and low price. Give each need an importance weight from 1 (barely matters) to 5 (must have). For the mess: taste 5, speed 3, price 4.

Next list technical responses, called the hows. These are things the team can change and measure, such as the menu cycle and the number of serving counters. Keep them at the design level; do not write a full solution.

Arrange needs as rows and responses as columns. This table, with importance and scores, is the house of quality. A need is a what; a response is a how. This is a different cut from functional vs non-functional requirements in 2.1: one customer need can lead to several functional and non-functional requirements, and a how is a design-level technical characteristic, not a requirement type. A vague need such as “good experience” is split into clear ones.
Each row-column cell gets a relationship score: 9 = strong, 3 = medium, 1 = weak, 0 = none. The score says how much the response supports that need. It is a rating, not rupees, days or a percentage.

blocks.where: P<sub>j</sub> is the priority score of response j (unitless); w<sub>i</sub> is the importance weight of customer need i; r<sub>ij</sub> is the relationship score between need i and response j. The sum runs over all needs i.

blocks.text: Do not add raw cells without weights. A 9 next to a weight-5 need counts more than a 9 next to a weight-3 need. Use 0 for no relationship; leave no cell blank.
Competitive assessment can compare your product with another product row by row. It is useful, but not needed for the basic score.

sections.h3: Read the ranking, not just the total

blocks.text: The weighted score ranks responses. Higher P<sub>j</sub> means the response supports more important needs more strongly. Start engineering work there. Use the score to discuss priorities with customers and developers, not to prove satisfaction.

A score is relative to this matrix. Add a new response or change a weight, and the ranking can change. If a response column is all zeros, it supports no listed need; question why it is in the plan. If a need has all zero cells, no response addresses it; the requirement is at risk.

QFD does not estimate cost, effort or schedule. Those belong to cost estimation (see Unit 6, Effort and cost estimation). The correlation roof and full competitive analysis are for a quality-management course. A tie is broken by the more important customer need or by a separate cost review. In an exam, draw only the matrix asked.

figure.caption: The QFD matrix for the hostel mess, with need weights in brackets: the menu cycle (M) column gives 5×9 + 3×1 + 4×3 = 60 and ranks first; counters (C) give 44.

spec.title: House of quality: hostel mess
spec.aria: A QFD array for the hostel mess with rows Taste (weight 5), Speed (3) and Price (4), columns M (menu cycle) and C (counters), relationship strengths 9,1,1,9,3,3, and priority scores 60 for menu cycle and 44 for counters.

examples.question: A hostel mess has weights: tasty food 5, quick service 3, low price 4. Responses are menu cycle and counter count. Strengths: taste-menu 9, taste-counters 1; speed-menu 1, speed-counters 9; price-menu 3, price-counters 3. Compute both priority scores and rank.
steps: 60 > 44, so menu cycle ranks first; scores are unitless.
examples.answer: Menu cycle ranks first with priority score 60; counter count scores 44.
examples.check:
weights = [5, 3, 4]
menu_strengths = [9, 1, 3]
counter_strengths = [1, 9, 3]
menu_score = sum(w * r for w, r in zip(weights, menu_strengths))
counter_score = sum(w * r for w, r in zip(weights, counter_strengths))
print(menu_score)
print(counter_score)

traps: Adding row or column cells without the customer importance weights.
Treating a relationship score as a cost, duration or percentage.
Marking every relationship 9, so the matrix cannot rank responses.
Confusing customer needs (what) with technical responses (how); a high score only sets priority, not satisfaction.

quiz.q: In QFD, what are the what and the how?
quiz.a: The what is a customer need; the how is a technical response the team can change.

quiz.q: Why are importance weights needed in the relationship matrix?
quiz.a: Weights make a strong relationship to an important need count more than the same strength for a minor need.

quiz.q: Using the worked example, state the menu-cycle score and the rank of the response scoring 44.
quiz.a: Menu cycle = 60; the response scoring 44 ranks second.

quiz.q: Why is a relationship score of 9 not a cost of ₹9 or 9 days?
quiz.a: It is a strength rating; it carries no unit and is multiplied by an importance weight, not by money or time.

quiz.q: What does a column of zeros mean?
quiz.a: The technical response supports none of the listed customer needs, so its priority is zero.

quiz.q: A team writes 9 in every cell. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Every response gets the same score (9 × the sum of the weights), so the ranking cannot guide effort; it also hides weak relationships and wastes work.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry QFD appears in product planning, service design and requirements workshops, often with the Kano model and voice-of-customer research. Software teams use light matrices to prioritise non-functional requirements. Search next for “house of quality”, “QFD voice of customer” and “Kano model”.
